query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the ability to form and maintain a stable, coherent protective oxide scale at temperatures above 900 °C is primarily controlled by the segregation behavior and preferential oxidation of the X element. Specifically, when X = Si the alloy forms an interfacial, Si-enriched oxide (potentially a mix of Cr2O3 and SiO2) that is chemically and thermally coherent with the substrate; in contrast, when X = Mn or Al, either the less compatible oxidation products (e.g., Mn-rich oxides) or a faster-growing, multi-layered oxide system are promoted, leading to internal stresses that cause cracking or spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys in a single- or multiphase solid-solution state with X being Si, Mn, or Al.
generation.intervention: Comparative in-situ thermal treatment experiments involving rapid exposure to 900+ °C in both oxidative (air or controlled O2-containing atmospheres) and non-oxidative (vacuum) environments, with phase evolution monitored by high-temperature X-ray diffraction (HTXRD) and compositional profiling.
generation.conditions: Exposure above 900 °C in a controlled oxidative or corrosive atmosphere versus a vacuum baseline; comparison across alloy variants where only the X element is altered.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a chemically homogeneous, interfacially-adherent oxide layer (e.g., a mixed Cr2O3/SiO2 layer for X = Si) versus a heterogeneous, layered oxide structure (e.g., Mn- or Al-rich oxides that might mis-match the alloy substrate in lattice parameters and thermal expansion).
generation.mechanism: Preferential oxidation of elements (Cr and X) controls the nature of the oxide scale. In alloys with X = Si, the slow-growing and chemically stable oxides along with beneficial element segregation promote formation of a coherent, adherent scale. In contrast, in alloys with X = Mn or Al, rapid and less coherent oxidation leads to the buildup of stresses (due to mismatch in thermal expansion or phase transformation volume changes) which ultimately results in oxide cracking or spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with X = Si will form a stable, continuous and coherent protective oxide layer that persists over time at high temperatures. Alloys with X = Mn or Al will form less coherent, rapidly growing oxide layers that tend to crack or spall due to increased interfacial stress and structural mismatch.
generation.baseline: The oxidation behavior observed in a vacuum (i.e., minimal oxidation) and/or comparison against well-characterized Cr-rich oxide formation in similar high-entropy alloys without the X element modification serves as the baseline.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to high-entropy alloys in single- or multiphase solid-solution states exposed to temperatures exceeding 900 °C under sustained oxidative or corrosive conditions. It is limited to the specific X substitutions (Si, Mn, or Al) and may not directly extrapolate to alloys with other minor alloying additions or different microstructures.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative impact of each X element on oxide growth kinetics and the degree of stress accumulation is uncertain, as is the potential influence of minor phase segregation in multiphase alloys. Further in-situ experiments and CALPHAD modeling are needed to refine the quantitative predictions.

falsification_experiment.design: Subject samples of CrFeCoNiX alloys (with X = Si, Mn, and Al) to identical high-temperature oxidation protocols (above 900 °C) under controlled oxidative atmospheres, while concurrently performing in-situ HTXRD to monitor phase evolution and ex-situ surface characterization (using SEM/EDS and XPS) to evaluate oxide layer continuity and composition. In addition, a parallel set conducted in vacuum will serve as baseline for oxidation-independent behavior.
measurements: Surface morphology and continuity via SEM
Chemical composition and depth profiling via EDS/XPS
Thermal and mechanical stress analysis (if possible) of the oxide layers
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If alloys with X = Si do not show formation of a coherent, stable oxide layer — or if alloys with X = Mn or Al unexpectedly develop a similarly coherent and protective oxide scale — then the hypothesis that the specific X element governs the protective oxide scale formation mechanism by preferential segregation and oxidation would be falsified.
